reconcile.connective: The Geneva annotators read Jesus's Matthew 20:23 disclaimer as addressing only his humbled human nature, leaving his divine omnipotence untouched.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain sense: a Jesus without power to assign thrones or heal in Nazareth cannot also claim 'all power.'

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How much power did Jesus have?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/power.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How much power did Jesus have?" (online, live by 2000)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The almightiness of Christ his divinity is not shut out by this, but it showeth the debasing of himself by taking man’s nature upon him.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the 'is not mine to give' disclaimer by locating it in Christ's assumed human nature while expressly denying it excludes his divine omnipotence — the same two-natures move that explains why he can later say 'all power is given unto me' (Matt 28:18) and why unbelief, not incapacity, limited him at Nazareth (Mark 6:5).

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 110-111 ("Omnipotence")
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under the heading 'Omnipotence — Had all power / Was not almighty,' Haley juxtaposes these same four texts (Matt 28:18, John 3:35 vs. Matt 20:23, Mark 6:5) directly against each other and resolves Matt 20:23 as a question of fitness rather than power ('the question is not one of power at all, but of fitness'), and Mark 6:5 as moral rather than physical impossibility, citing Grotius, Chrysostom, Clarke, Barnes, and Alford. (Verified via full-text search of the 1874 edition on archive.org.)
